stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

sources.title: How to build a software factory with 7 Claude Fable Agents
How to Build a Software Factory with Claude Code: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Development

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: Poolside's Founders Reverse-Acquihire to NVIDIA in $12B Deal
stories.summary: AI News reports that AI coding startup Poolside struck a $12 billion deal with NVIDIA. The founders stay at Poolside and receive $1 billion. Poolside's employees move to NVIDIA for a combined $6 billion. The report also says Poolside's infrastructure arm, Infraco, plans to scale its "neocloud" capacity to 7 gigawatts.
stories.whyItMatters: The deal shows NVIDIA using cash and compute leverage to absorb AI talent and infrastructure. This pattern could reshape who controls AI compute capacity.
whatToWatch: Confirmation of the deal terms from Poolside or NVIDIA
Progress on Infraco's 7GW neocloud buildout
Reaction from other AI infrastructure and coding-model startups
questions: What happens to Poolside's existing products under the new structure?
How much of the $12 billion is cash versus compute credits or equity?

sources.title: [AINews] Poolside gets $12B reverse-execuhire to NVIDIA; founders stay for $1B, employees go for $6B, Infraco scaling to 7GW neocloud

stories.title: [AINews] 10% worse, 100x cheaper, 10000x faster: Why Simulation is taking over
stories.summary: The latest Latent Space AI News roundup argues that simulation is spreading because it trades a small accuracy loss for large savings. It cites simulation as roughly 10% worse than the alternative but about 100 times cheaper and 10,000 times faster. The summary does not name which specific systems or benchmarks back these numbers.
stories.whyItMatters: If cheap, fast simulation keeps closing the accuracy gap, AI teams may shift more work from real-world data collection to simulated data and testing.
whatToWatch: Which companies or products the newsletter cites as evidence
Follow-up coverage that quantifies the trade-off
questions: What tasks or domains do the '10% worse' figures apply to?
Is this a broad trend or specific to one type of AI system?

sources.title: [AINews] 10% worse, 100x cheaper, 10000x faster: Why Simulation is taking over

stories.title: How the AI 'Agent Harness' Has Evolved
stories.summary: A Latent Space piece traces the evolution of the "agent harness" — the tooling and orchestration layer that lets large language models act as autonomous agents. It is framed as a retrospective on how this layer has changed as agentic AI products matured.
stories.whyItMatters: The harness layer shapes how reliable and useful AI agents are in practice, so changes to it affect every product built on top of foundation models.
whatToWatch: Which harness designs or vendors the piece highlights
Whether the patterns it describes become a common standard
questions: Does the piece point to one dominant harness design, or many competing ones?

sources.title: The Evolution of the Agent Harness

stories.title: OzBrain Launches as a Shared Knowledge Base for AI Agents and Teams
stories.summary: A developer introduced OzBrain on Hacker News's Show HN. It is described as a shared "brain" that stores knowledge for both AI agents and human team members to use. The project targets teams that mix AI agents with human colleagues and want one common memory layer.
stories.whyItMatters: Shared memory between agents and humans is a common pain point in agentic workflows, so new tools here matter to teams adopting AI agents at work.
whatToWatch: Community feedback and adoption on Hacker News
Whether the project opens its source code
questions: How does OzBrain control access between team members and agents?
What sets it apart from existing agent memory tools?

sources.title: Show HN: OzBrain, a shared brain for knowledge between agents and your team

stories.title: A Developer's Blueprint for a Self-Hosted, Sandboxed 'Agentic Software Factory'
stories.summary: A Hacker News-featured blog post describes one developer's build of an almost fully self-hosted, sandboxed system for agentic software development. It works as a pipeline of AI coding agents running in isolated environments. The post is a personal, hands-on account, not a company announcement.
stories.whyItMatters: Independent builders working out self-hosted agent pipelines point to growing demand for AI coding setups that do not depend on closed, hosted platforms.
whatToWatch: Whether others fork or adopt the approach
Follow-up posts with performance or reliability results
questions: How does the sandboxing keep agents safe when they write and run code?

sources.title: Building an (almost) fully self-hosted, sandboxed, agentic software factory

stories.title: Google DeepMind Asks What 'Full-Stack' AI Really Means
stories.summary: Google DeepMind published a blog post that examines what the term "full-stack" AI means. Companies increasingly use this phrase to describe controlling everything from chips to models to applications. The post reads as an explainer, not a product announcement.
stories.whyItMatters: AI companies compete partly on how much of the stack they control. How this term gets defined shapes comparisons between Google and its rivals.
whatToWatch: Whether Google ties this framing to specific upcoming products
How rivals respond to or adopt the 'full-stack' framing
questions: Does Google, by its own definition, call itself more 'full-stack' than rivals like OpenAI or Microsoft?

stories.title: Simile AI's Joon Sung Park Argues Simulation Is a New Scaling Law
stories.summary: In a Latent Space interview, Joon Sung Park of Simile AI argues that simulation is a new kind of scaling law for AI. He places it alongside the more familiar data- and compute-scaling laws. The discussion frames simulation as a distinct lever for improving AI systems.
stories.whyItMatters: Scaling laws have driven major investment decisions across the AI industry. A credible new scaling axis could redirect where compute and research effort go next.
whatToWatch: Whether other researchers or labs adopt 'simulation scaling' as a framework
Concrete results from Simile AI that support the claim
questions: What evidence supports simulation as a scaling law rather than just a useful technique?
How does Simile AI define and measure simulation scale?

sources.title: Simulation: the new Scaling Law — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI

stories.title: Opinion: LLMs Prove the Unix Philosophy Won
stories.summary: A personal blog post, featured on Hacker News, argues that the success of large language models proves the Unix philosophy won. That philosophy favors small, composable tools that work together. The piece is an opinion essay, not a news report.
stories.whyItMatters: The argument offers a lens on why simple, composable designs around LLMs, such as text pipes and tool calls, have proven durable. This matters to anyone building AI tooling.
whatToWatch: Discussion and pushback in the Hacker News comment thread
questions: Does the argument hold for multimodal AI systems, not just text-based ones?

sources.title: LLMs are proof that Unix won

stories.title: A Personal Account of Writing a Paper With Leslie Lamport
stories.summary: Computer scientist Lawrence Paulson published a personal blog post, shared on Hacker News. It recounts how he came to co-write a paper with Leslie Lamport, known for foundational work on distributed systems and formal verification. The post is a personal reflection, not new research.
stories.whyItMatters: Formal verification work of the kind linked to Lamport increasingly connects to efforts to make AI systems more reliable and provable. This history interests readers who follow that thread.
questions: What was the paper about, and does it bear on current formal-verification work?

sources.title: How I came to write that paper with Leslie Lamport

stories.title: AI News Digest: 'Not Much Happened Today'
stories.summary: The smol.ai AI News digest for August 21 carried the headline "not much happened today." This reflects a rare quiet stretch in AI industry news. No major releases, deals, or policy moves are noted for the period.
stories.whyItMatters: Even a quiet day is useful signal for readers who track the pace of AI news. It shows the release cycle can pause.
whatToWatch: Whether the pace of news picks back up in the next digest
